extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, inventors, and corporate counsel prosecuting or litigating U.S. patents involving AI
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining inventorship, disclosure duties, and prosecution practices for inventions developed using AI in U.S. patent applications, including how to apply joint-inventor standards and the Pannu factors to AI-assisted inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventors and Joint Inventors Must Be Natural Persons
rubrics_metrics.description: An AI system cannot be named as an inventor or joint inventor on a U.S. patent; inventorship analysis should focus on human contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although AI-assisted inventions are not categorically unpatentable, only natural persons should be identified as inventors and an invention developed using AI cannot be patented unless a natural person qualifies as an inventor under existing standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural-Person Significant Contribution Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentability depends on the involvement of a natural person in the conception and development of the claimed invention such that a natural person must, for each claim, at least meet the standards for naming a joint inventor—i.e., a natural person must significantly contribute to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For AI-assisted inventions, traditional joint-inventor/conception standards apply; a natural person must significantly contribute to each claim (see Pannu factors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the Pannu Factors to Determine Inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO will apply the Pannu factors to decide whether a potential joint inventor 'contribute[d] in some significant manner to conception or reduction to practice,' made 'a contribution to the claimed invention that is not insignificant in quality, when that contribution is measured against the dimension of the full invention,' and did more than merely explain well-known concepts or the current state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three Pannu-factor questions as the threshold joint-inventorship inquiry for AI-assisted inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition and Appreciation Requirement for Conception
rubrics_metrics.description: At least one natural person must have 'recognition and appreciation' of the invention; where there is only a single human inventor of an AI-assisted invention, that natural person must have the necessary recognition and appreciation of the entire invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditional notions of conception apply to AI-assisted inventions—recognition and appreciation of the invention are required to show conception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Per-Claim Human Contribution Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: At least one natural person must significantly contribute to each and every patent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike typical joint-inventor rules (where not every named inventor must contribute to every claim), for AI-assisted inventions at least one natural person must significantly contribute to every claim; claims cannot cover inventions developed solely by an AI system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding Principle i — AI as Tool Does Not Negate Human Contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of an AI system as a tool does not necessarily negate a natural person's contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A natural person can be named as an inventor so long as that person significantly contributes to the claimed AI-assisted invention and other patentability requirements are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding Principle ii — Mere Problem Recognition Is Insufficient; Prompt Construction May Count
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere recognition and presentation of a problem to an AI system is not itself sufficient to rise to conception, but 'a significant contribution could be shown by the way the person constructs the prompt in view of a specific problem to elicit a particular solution from the AI system.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How a prompt is constructed can be evidence of significant contribution; simply stating the problem to an AI is generally insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding Principle iii — Reduction to Practice Alone Is Insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduction to practice of AI output (e.g., recognizing the output as an invention or implementing it) alone is not enough to establish inventorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A natural person who merely reduces AI-produced output to practice is not necessarily an inventor, unless they made a significant contribution to producing the output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding Principle iv — Developing an Essential Building Block Can Be Sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: A natural person who develops an essential building block from which the claimed invention is derived may be considered to have provided significant contribution to conception even if not present for each activity that led to the invention; designing, constructing, or training an AI system for a specific issue could qualify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individuals who design/train an AI system specifically to generate a targeted solution may qualify as inventors when that work constitutes a significant part of the process that leads to the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding Principle v — Ownership or Oversight Alone Is Insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Ownership or oversight (maintaining 'intellectual domination') of an AI system alone is not enough to make a natural person an inventor of inventions created through its use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A natural person must contribute beyond mere ownership or supervision to be an inventor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenario 1 — Not Inventors If They Simply Applied AI Output
rubrics_metrics.description: Engineers who recognized a problem and input a general prompt into an AI system and then simply applied the AI's original design are not proper inventors of a claim covering only the AI system’s design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition of a problem plus application of an AI-generated design without significant contribution to the design does not satisfy inventorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenario 2 — Not Inventors If Only Reduction to Practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Engineers who follow the AI system’s design exactly and only select a common manufacturing material (i.e., merely reduce the output to practice) are not proper inventors of dependent claim limitations reflecting those choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting routine manufacturing choices does not create inventorship for AI-derived claim limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenario 3 — Proper Inventors If They Substantially Modify the AI Output
rubrics_metrics.description: Engineers who prompt the AI for alternatives and conduct experiments that allow them to substantially modify the AI output may be proper inventors of an independent claim covering the modified design because the Pannu factors are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantial modification and empirical work that produces a materially different, inventive result can support inventorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenario 4 — Proper Inventors of Dependent Claims When Contributions Remain Significant
rubrics_metrics.description: Engineers who develop a modified design (as in Scenario 3) and then use AI suggestions for manufacturing may still be proper inventors of dependent claims covering the AI suggestions because their prior contributions remain significant when measured against the full invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A human's earlier significant contributions can support inventorship of later-related dependent claim limitations even if those limitations draw on AI suggestions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenario 5 — AI System Developer Is Not Inventor If Unaware of Specific Problem
rubrics_metrics.description: An engineer who oversaw creation and training of an AI system but was unaware of any specific problems addressed (e.g., transaxle issues) is not a proper inventor because they did not significantly contribute to conception of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General development or training of an AI system without targeted work toward the particular inventive solution is insufficient for inventorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Related Inventorship Issue — Duty of Disclosure and Reasonable Inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants have a duty to disclose to the USPTO information that raises a prima facie case of unpatentability due to improper inventorship, including evidence that a named inventor did not significantly contribute because the purported invention was made by an AI system; applicants must investigate the use of AI when circumstances warrant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to inquire or disclose AI involvement when warranted may jeopardize application validity or enforceability and could result in sanctions; improper inventorship can be a ground for rejection under 35 U.S.C. §§ 101 and 115.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign Priority Inventorship Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A foreign priority application must name at least one common natural person inventor for the foreign application to be used for U.S. patenting; a foreign application that names an AI system as sole inventor will not be accepted for priority purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: U.S. and foreign priority filings must share at least one natural-person inventor; AI cannot be the named inventor on a foreign application if priority is to be claimed in the U.S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping and Documentation Recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventors using AI systems should keep detailed records and document their inventive process to help establish conception and significant contribution, including the natural person’s specific prompts to the AI system, the AI system’s specific output, and any changes made by the inventor to the output, on a claim-by-claim basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed contemporaneous records will be important to establish inventorship, defend validity, and guard against inequitable conduct allegations; prosecution counsel should draft claims to preserve the natural person's significant contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution and Litigation Implications — Increased Inventorship Challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Improper inventorship will present a new front for challenging validity of patents claiming AI-assisted inventions before the PTAB and in district court litigation; parties should evaluate inventorship on both sides of adversarial proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counsel should proactively assess inventorship risk in prosecution and litigation strategy and consider potential challenges based on AI involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance Scope — Applies to All U.S. Patents and Applications
rubrics_metrics.description: The Inventorship Guidance applies to all U.S. patents and applications and provides guidelines for determining whether and when a natural person may be named as an inventor on an invention made in whole or in part using AI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The principles and requirements described should be applied across U.S. filings; the USPTO may issue additional guidance on related AI issues (subject-matter eligibility, obviousness, enablement) in future.
